title: Rivers Never Dry

<div class="chapter-three">

##### Sohyun Jun

# Rivers Never Dry

<div class="body-text">

As the human population has grown exponentially, urban areas have expanded rapidly over recent decades. Cities were home to roughly 45% of the global population in 2015, up from 20% in 1950, and built-up urban land is expanding faster than population growth across many regions.1 The majority of human and economic activity is now concentrated in cities. As part of this urban growth and economic concentration, London, one of the biggest cities on earth, experienced rapid urbanisation during the Industrial Revolution. As rural populations moved into the city to work in factories, London was challenged in its capacity to function effectively. One example is waste management: the bigger the city gets, the more waste is produced. The widespread discharge of sewage into waterways effectively turned the rivers in London into an open sewer, spreading disease and causing recurring health crises. In response, many of the rivers feeding into the Thames were buried underground, or culverted, by the local government in reaction. Until now, although they seem dry, these rivers are still flowing beneath our feet, repurposed as sewers.

<img src="/static/images/Soyhun/image1.png" class="single-column-img">

Figure 1\. Alder trees at Belair Park, sited on the Effra's former course.

The project started from curiosity that emerged from the observation of our urban environment. I have participated in the _Lost Rivers of South London cycling tour_ from Open City, cycling around Clapham Junction, Brixton, and Vauxhall areas, with a historian and other participants.2 During the tour, the strong collective interests in the invisible rivers made visible what has been transformed into something else: parks occupying land too damp for habitation; willow and alder trees quietly marking the former channel; buildings built to avoid the buried riverbed; and Victorian stink pipes emerging awkwardly between roads and buildings.3

<img src="/static/images/Soyhun/image2.png" class="single-column-img">

Figure 2\. Historical map of the River Effra (left) and GPS walking data imported into Google Maps (right).

Twenty of the thirty-eight tributaries that once flowed into the Thames are now culverted and erased from the surface. I decided to narrow it down to a specific location and investigate the underground river through walking, a more embodied experience. I visited sites along the River Effra, which once flowed through south-west London from Crystal Palace, Dulwich, Brixton, and then to Vauxhall. I walked from the upstream source at Crystal Palace, following the old map, with my Apple Watch turned on, intending to record my body data: timestamp, latitude, longitude, heart rate, speed, and elevation (Figure 2). Contrary to my expectation, the relation between my speed, heart rate, and elevation wasn't very strong. The data was too noisy, as I got lost, took photographs, and rested along the way. However, this way of researching gave me a deeper connection to the landscape and to the changes in surroundings. I converted this data of 6 hours 59 minutes 38 seconds, 14.5 km, 25,359 steps into lines, and stacked them on top of a 3D model of London's terrain. I then combined the three lines by multiplying them together, then applied the resulting value as a 'height' field to a flat plane to generate a new surface. Rather than raising the surface where this value was high, I inverted it so the surface sank instead, simulating erosion in the way a river carves into land over time (Figure 3). Could this be an alternative way of sensing the entity, one that can no longer be sensed directly, as it is now considered biologically 'dead'?  
<img src="/static/images/Soyhun/image3.png" class="single-column-img">

Figure 3\. Walking data mapped in a 3D environment.

Another mode of existence of the lost rivers has emerged as public data. Over the past few years, Thames Water has made real-time storm discharge data publicly accessible, and I was able to successfully query this through their API. Publication of this dataset was a result of the public attention to the transparency of sewage spills into the rivers.4 In this array of data, it shows 576 monitored locations in total, across the whole Thames Water operating area from around Hampshire in the west to Essex in the east. At each location, the most interesting information was whether it was currently discharging, the most recent time it discharged, and the receiving water course. It was the moment when the subterranean rivers emerged into a broader ecological setting and were translated into data. Monitoring data from the sensing point near the Effra outfall at _Cadogan Pier_, provided by the Environment Agency (EA), I was able to identify relations between storm discharge activity and water quality data coming from different sources. For example, there was a storm discharge event into the Thames on 2 June 2026, reported by Thames Water. Checking the water quality data from the EA, I found that on 3 June 2026, the dissolved oxygen level dropped (Figure 4, 5). Was this the result of the sewage discharge? If so, why did the drop in oxygen level take a day? As _Cadogan Pier_ is located a little upstream of the Effra outfall, you might think the influence of this activity would be limited. But in fact, the Thames is a tidal river, or rather, a complex living organism, where what happens at one local point can result in a chain of damage in delay.

<img src="/static/images/Soyhun/image4.png" class="single-column-img">

Figure 4\. Storm discharge data for the South West Storm Relief CSO, retrieved from the Thames Water API on 7 June 2026\.

<img src="/static/images/Soyhun/image5.png" class="single-column-img">

Figure 5\. Decline in dissolved oxygen levels on 03 June 2026 at Cadogan Pier. Screenshot from the Environment Agency website ([https://environment.data.gov.uk/hydrology/CADOG2](https://environment.data.gov.uk/hydrology/CADOG2)).

Scientific research articles indicate that the spike in conductivity combined with drops in dissolved oxygen are classic indicators of organic pollution. Bacteria breaking down the waste consume a large amount of oxygen, driving dissolved oxygen levels down. As dissolved oxygen levels go down, the water becomes acidic, and decomposing organic waste dissolves into basic chemical ions, raising conductivity and salinity.5 After this traumatic incident, the river will replenish its oxygen through turbulence and the photosynthetic activity of plants and algae over time.

<img src="/static/images/Soyhun/image6.png" class="single-column-img">

Figure 6\. Data collection points across different data sources (Environment Agency API, Thames Water API).

Compared to scientific journals that have demonstrated correlations through long-term research using the methods verified in a standardised manner, my casual discovery in the corner of my room, as it happens, proves nothing. What I am attempting is something different. Gabrys and Pritchard from Sensing Practice propose that sensing need not be understood as a human mind decoding an external world, but as experience expressed through subjects in relation.6 Through this research, I am attempting to look through the river’s mind and become one of its network actors.

This real-time data serves to highlight the presence of these fragmented rivers even more profoundly. The rivers were detected, digitised and transmitted via satellite, before being distributed to personal computers via the cloud. Whilst this may appear to be nothing more than cold, hard figures, it encompasses far more than mere information: it embodies political and social contexts, the history of human activity unfolding across the land, and the countless cycles of trauma and recovery that have unfolded in between. It is much like how the rivers that have vanished from the London terrain are still felt through the various entities associated with them.

This research is developing into an installation. This kinetic piece, which focuses on material structures continuously changing through movement, is to be constructed using industrial pipes and custom 3D-printed fittings and bases. The decision to leave the structure exposed rather than concealed was intended to suggest that the river, whilst no longer visible as a body of water, continues to exist in another form; the custom-made connectors, which reinterpret the Victorian designs found in ‘stink pipes’ and pumping stations, point to not only the human engineering that caused geological reformation but also the entangled network of relations that continues to branch out in a rhizomatic direction, much as Bruno Latour proposed that non-human entities such as technologies, objects, and natural elements continually shape society and the outcomes.7 This structure consists of three motors connected in series — each motor moves in response to real-time water quality and storm discharge data, and their individually determined movements ultimately form a single, unique shape of structure, symbolising the ongoing interplay between the river’s ecosystem and infrastructure as they seek to regulate one another.

Living in the age of the Anthropocene, it is not just the number of species that is being reduced, but entire ways of feeling, thinking, acting, and being.8 Collaborating with machines to sense the non-human, such as the river, and the trees and land around it, gave me the opportunity to understand and rethink the way human supremacy has been working in our current world, and its resilience against it. Using the technologies accessible to me at the moment, and collecting 'just good enough data', I suggest we question, react to, create with, and interpret this data, turning it into a more democratised form of monitoring and engaging stories that might ordinarily not be documented.9

Lost rivers still redirect water, shape the ground, and give homes to countless life forms. Transformed into a data stream, they exert physical and social effects. Knowing this, can we really say they have dried up?
